name: Beauty micrometer

lead: The Beauty Micrometer, also called the Beauty Calibrator, was a mask-like metal device made by Max Factor in the early 1930s. It fitted over the face and measured contours so that small flaws, which could look magnified on camera, could be found and covered with makeup.
Its appearance payoff was targeted makeup correction for film stars. Wikipedia describes it as a device to detect barely visible structural flaws, and Grokipedia says only one prototype was made.

paras: Per Grokipedia, adjustable screws and flexible strips formed a frame that traced the face; technicians then used the readings to place corrective makeup, such as evening out nose and forehead heights.
It was a measuring device with no medical effect. Grokipedia describes its approach as pseudo-scientific and its use as limited to film studios and beauty parlors.

angle.text: The device located facial irregularities so makeup could correct them on camera. It is a historical forerunner of facial-proportion analysis.

lead: The Beauty Micrometer was a mask-like measuring device developed by Max Factor in the 1930s to detect barely visible structural flaws in a subject's face, which a technician could then mask with makeup [1].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, dates it to 1932 and says it had 325 adjustable screws and flexible metal strips to map facial contours to a thousandth of an inch, and compares it to calipers and engineering micrometers. It says it was meant to guide makeup so that, for example, nose and forehead heights matched [2].
Grokipedia says it echoed phrenology and anthropometry, was tried on actress Dorothy Wilson in 1933, and that its single surviving example is at The Hollywood Museum [2].

paras: Max Factor founded his cosmetics firm in Los Angeles in 1909 and became a leading Hollywood makeup innovator [2]. Wikipedia's Max Factor article notes the micrometer was a mask-like device for measuring face contours [1].

timeline.event: Demonstrated on Dorothy Wilson, per Grokipedia [2].
